From these results, it is confirmed that the generally reported peaks at ca. 285.0–285.4 eV for carbon materials prepared at high temperatures are most likely not sp 3 C for many reports as mentioned in our previous work (Fig.  14 a) [ 80 ,  114 ], if the origin of the peak at ca. 285 eV is not charged-up sp 3 C, C–N, or adventitious carbon. For the adventitious carbon, it has been utilized as a reference peak, C=C, to adjust peak shifts in other orbitals in the field of inorganic chemistry and solid catalysts. However, the influence of adventitious carbon in carbon materials on C1s XPS spectra is negligible from the results of our previous works [ 52 ,  53 ,  73 ] since the amount of carbon in carbon materials compared to adventitious carbon is abundant. For the sp 3 C, it is unstable at high temperatures in the absence of pressure [ 123 ,  124 ]. Thus, consideration of neither adventitious carbon nor charged-up sp 3 C is necessary for general electrically conducting carbon materials prepared at high temperatures such as isotropic pitch-based carbon fiber in this work. Our results showed that the peak position of the peak generally reported as sp 3 C is close to the peak position of Defect2 (285.1–285.4 eV) containing 66V, 56V, and 668C=C (Fig.  14 a). The obtained information is extremely valuable since there are millions of repots about sp 3 C in C1s XPS spectra for carbon materials. This result also holds significant meaning because most carbon materials form non-hexagonal rings during carbonization [ 73 ,  81 ] and most of these non-hexagonal rings are difficult to remove completely even at high temperatures [ 122 ].

This work also clarified that the broadening of C=C originates from C=C influenced by functional groups in addition to the non-hexagonal rings, although our previous work explained the broadening [ 112 ,  121 ]. The influenced C=C bonds, which are not directly bonded to oxygen, are predominantly observed  when oxygen-containing functional groups are present near the C=C bonds ( C =C=O,  C =COH, and  C =C-O-C in Fig.  13 bviii, xi, and xvi). The FWHMs of the total peaks of C1s XPS spectra are also shown in Fig.  13 a. The FWHMs of graphene with one type of non-hexagonal rings such as pentagons or heptagons [ 94 ,  115 ] or those with either Stone–Thrower–Wales defects, point defect with cyclic ether, and various oxygen-containing functional groups were investigated [ 112 ,  121 ]. However, the influence of mixed hexagonal and two kinds of non-hexagonal rings on the FWHMs on the C=C peak positions other than those defects has not been previously clarified. In this work, the influence of various defects on FWHMs was calculated. The FWHM of the peak of the total C1s XPS spectrum of defect-free graphene other than edges (1.1 eV (Fig.  13 ai)) increased with the introduction of most defects except for four C=O groups (Fig.  13 aiii). The FWHMs of the peaks of C=C of C1s XPS spectra are further shown in Fig.  13 a. Thus, depending on the types of oxygen-containing functional groups, the influence on the FWHM of C=C differs. The FWHMs of the peak of C=C of C1s XPS spectrum of defect-free graphene other than edges (1.1 eV (Fig.  13 ai)) increased with the introduction of six cyclic ether groups (1.2 eV (Fig.  13 axvi and xvii)), 5-8-5 defects (1.3 eV (Fig.  13 axxvi)), and grain boundary (1.2 eV (Fig.  13 aiv)). Therefore, the presence of cyclic ethers, pentagons, heptagons, and octagons influenced the peak positions of C=C in C1s XPS, which is one of the causes of the broadening of C1s XPS spectra. The presence of vacancy defects (Fig.  13 axxiv) did not influence the FWHM of C=C (1.1 eV) since the bonding state of graphene with a vacancy defect (Fig.  13 axxiv) is similar to that with only edges (Fig.  13 ai).

The dependence of the shift of C1s XPS spectra on the types of aromatic rings surrounding the analyzed carbon atoms was similar to that of N1s XPS spectra on the types of aromatic rings surrounding the analyzed tertiary nitrogen atoms, so-called graphitic nitrogen, in graphene with hexagonal rings and non-hexagonal rings [ 122 ]. Our previous work roughly revealed the influence of the non-hexagonal rings, but the details on the peak shift related to the summed number of three rings surrounding the tertiary nitrogen for N1s XPS spectra were not clear. In this work, we revisit the discussion about the peak positions of tertiary nitrogen influenced by non-hexagonal rings again because this trend is historically important and not widely recognized by other researchers. The peak positions of N1s XPS spectra for tertiary nitrogen are in the order of 566N < 567N < 666N < 667N [ 122 ] (Fig.  14 a). Thus, in a similar way to our previous work for N1s XPS spectra, our group solved the problems of C1s XPS spectra of carbon materials in this work.

From the plots in Fig.  14 b, a summed number of three rings, 20 (e.g., from configuration of three rings such as 677C=C, 578C=C, and 668C=C), is required to reach ca. 285 eV. In short, those generally reported peak positions at ca. 285 eV as sp 3 C could originate from heptagons or larger rings, point defects, C–N bonds, or charged-up sp 3 C for samples prepared at low heat treatment temperatures. Conversely, for samples prepared at high heat treatment temperatures, these peaks likely originate from heptagons, larger rings, or point defects. Furthermore, this work highlights the importance of future studies for carbon materials containing heptagons or larger rings in combination with heteroatoms.

The trend of the peak shift of C=C in C1s XPS spectra has been roughly explained by our group from the point of view of Mulliken charge [ 94 ,  115 ,  117 ], but some of the results could not be fully explained, possibly because of the influence of neighboring surrounding rings [ 81 ,  119 ]. For example, the peak position of C=C in one pentagon surrounded by five hexagons (corannulene) is clearly different from that in one pentagon surrounded by three hexagons (fluoranthene) [ 81 ]. It is well known that carbon atoms on pentagons tend to be electron-rich, which lowers the binding energy. In contrast, those on heptagons tend to be electron-poor, resulting in a higher binding energy [ 94 ,  117 ]. From the trend in Fig.  14 b, it is suggested that the peak positions of atoms surrounded by three rings for C1s and N1s XPS spectra can be estimated by an averaging effect from the three surrounding rings.

sections.heading: Experimental XPS
paragraphs: Figures  15  and  S19  show experimental C1s and O1s XPS spectra of pitch after infusibilization and CF prepared at 773–3137 K, respectively. In addition, the C1s XPS spectra of the basal plane and the edge plane of HOPG are also shown as reference samples. These references were used to determine the narrowest FWHM and peak shapes determined by the ratio of the Lorentz and Gaussian function in the Voigt function [ 119 ], which is written as L/G in the figure and the asymmetry factor, which is written as α in the figure, as used in our previous works [ 95 ,  112 ,  118 ]. Estimating the spectral shapes is challenging unless the results of combustion elemental analysis are obtained and graphite with low defects such as HOPG is used. Thus, the results of combustion elemental analysis were applied and HOPG samples were analyzed. For example, the percentages of the peaks, such as C=C, C–H, and C–O/C=O, were determined based on the results of combustion elemental analysis (Tables  1  and S1) because it is known that it is extremely challenging to clarify the peak position of C=C in C1s XPS spectra of general carbon materials with various defects. Many works reported by our group have shown that the use of combustion elemental analysis data can estimate C=C positions [ 77 ,  80 ,  81 ,  92 ] although this method assumes that the compositions of the bulk and the surface of carbon materials are the same. Moreover, the difference in the percentage of deconvoluted C1s XPS spectra deviated from the averaged percentages of deconvoluted C1s XPS spectra is shown in Table  S2 . The percentage was obtained from spectra deconvoluted three times by changing L/G, α, and/or FWHM, and the averaged results are shown in Fig.  15 . Figure 15 Experimental C1s XPS spectra of pitch after infusibilization, CF prepared at 773–3173 K, and HOPG. The experimental peak top of C=C was adjusted at 284.3 eV in a similar way to the calculated peak top of C=C. Deconvolution was conducted three times, and the averaged percentages are shown in this figure. The numbers in parentheses are FWHMs of the peaks. The types of defects in Defect1, Defect2, and 5 ring are explained in Fig.  14 a. The data of pitch after infusibilization were obtained from our previous work [ 31 ], but reassigned in this work.

Once the peak positions and the ratios of C–H and C–O/C=O in C1s XPS spectra are fixed from O1s XPS spectra, L/G, and α, FWHM of each peak in C1s XPS spectra can be roughly fixed. The percentages of peaks of oxygen-containing functional groups in O1s XPS spectra can be applied to C1s XPS spectra at the following ratio: C:O = 1:1 for C–OH/C=O/C=O–O–C and C:O = 2:1 for C–O–C. In a similar way, the percentage of the peak of nitrogen-containing functional groups in N1s XPS spectra can be applied to C1s XPS spectra at the following ratio: C:N = 1:1 for C–NH 2 , C:N = 2:1 for C–N–C, and C:N = 3:1 for C–N–C 2  such as tertiary nitrogen. However, the peaks for C–N tend to overlap with the peaks for C=C in non-hexagonal rings. Thus, the accurate analysis of especially C–N peaks in the C1s spectrum is challenging.

Both experimental C1s XPS spectra of the basal plane and the edge plane of HOPG showed a similar spectral shape (Fig.  15 ). The calculated peak positions in Fig.  13  and Table  5  were referred to assign experimental peak positions. “Defect1” at 284.6 eV, “Defect2” at 285.1 eV, and “5 ring” at 283.9 eV, as shown in Fig.  15 , contain various defects as explained in Fig.  14 . In the temperature range where H was not detected in combustion elemental analysis (Table  1 ), the values of the Lorentz-to-Gaussian function (L/G) and α relate to the electrical conductivity of the sample [ 114 ,  119 ]. Thus, L/G and α values were obtained from the experimental spectral shapes of the basal plane of HOPG and set lower as the heat treatment temperature became lower. For the assignment method, the shape of C1s XPS spectra was first confirmed by HOPG, and then, the assignment of C1s XPS spectra of CF was performed from high preparation temperatures to low preparation temperatures, so that the changes in the peaks would become clear.

The FWHMs of experimental C1s XPS spectra for the basal plane and the edges of HOPG were both 1.1 eV, whereas those of CF prepared at 3173 K or lower were 1.2 eV or higher (Fig.  15 ), indicating that defects other than edges are clearly present in CF prepared at 3173 K or lower. The FWHMs of C1s XPS spectra of CF prepared at 2273 K or higher show little contribution from C–H, C–O, or C–N because the percentages of C–H, C–O, or C–N are smaller than the detection limit of combustion elemental analysis (0.1%) (Table  1 ). However, since a peak originating from C–O–C of mainly cyclic ether at 533.5 eV was clearly detected for O1s XPS spectra of CF 2773 K or higher by comparing with O1s XPS spectrum of HOPG edge (Fig.  S19 ), it is probable that cyclic ether is present in CF 3173 K, although this peak is also close to the peak position of either OH interacted with water by hydrogen bonding [ 120 ,  124 ] or non-cyclic ether [ 120 ]. The stability of cyclic ether in the subnanometer vacancy defects in graphene was explained to be high under the irradiation of an electron beam during transmission electron microscope observation [ 57 ], although it depends on the structure. Temperature-programmed desorption analysis of carbon material revealed that CO was observed slightly at 1500 K [ 153 ] or above [ 154 ], and the desorption of CO probably originates from cyclic ether. Another possibility is the adsorption of oxygen-containing species such as O 2  and H 2 O at the reactive sites after taking out samples from furnaces. In addition, determining the presence of the OH group is challenging unless a well-dried sample is inserted in the XPS device using a transfer vessel from a glove box since the peak overlaps with the peak of adsorbed water.

From the calculated results, for the experimental spectra of CF 2273–3173 K, the peak labeled “Defect1” at 284.6 eV should include grain boundaries and/or defects containing non-hexagonal rings such as heptagons, octagons, or larger ring defects with a total number of rings, 19, obtained by summing three rings surrounding the analyzed carbon atom,  e . g ., 667C=C and 568C=C. In contrast, the peak labeled “Defect2” at 285.1 eV includes grain boundaries and/or defects including heptagons or larger ring defects obtained by summing three rings surrounding the analyzed carbon atom,  e . g ., 677C=C and 578C=C in addition to 668C=C (Fig.  14 a). This is consistent with the results that almost no hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen are present in CF prepared at 2273–3173 K (Table  1 ). In short, CF prepared at 2273–3173 K is estimated to include grain boundaries and/or defects including heptagons or larger ring defects with the total number of rings being 20, which is obtained by summing three rings surrounding the analyzed carbon atom, and probably a small percentage of cyclic ether.

For the experimental spectrum of CF 1873 K, the peak labeled “Defect1” at 284.6 eV should include defects,  e . g ., C=C influenced by cyclic ether (C=COC) and C=O (C=C=O) in addition to 667C=C and 568C=C, whereas the peak labeled “Defect2” at 285.1 eV includes defects,  e . g ., 66V and 56V in addition to 668C=C, since almost no hydrogen but a small amount of oxygen (0.2 at.%) is included (Table  1 ). Mainly C=O and cyclic ether were observed in CF 1873 K (Fig.  S19 ). In short, CF 1873 K is estimated to include mainly C=O and cyclic ether in addition to grain boundaries and/or defects including heptagons or larger rings with the total number of rings, 20, obtained by summing three rings surrounding the analyzed carbon atom. The stability of the cyclic ether has been explained by calculating the activation energy [ 57 ].

For the experimental spectrum of CF 1473 K, the peak labeled “Defect1” at 284.6 eV should include defects such as,  e . g ., C=C influenced by functional groups (C=COC, C=C=O, and C=C–OH) in addition to 667C=C and 568C=C, whereas the peak labeled “Defect2” at 285.1 eV includes defects such as,  e . g ., 66V, 56V, and C–N [ 80 ,  92 ,  119 ] in addition to 668C=C. This is because almost no hydrogen but a small amount of oxygen is included (Table  1 ) and O1s XPS spectra show the presence of C–O–C and C=O in addition to C–OH/water (Fig.  S19 ). Thus, the peak at 286.3 eV mainly contains C–O–C, C=O, and/or C–OH [ 95 ,  112 ,  120 ].

At 1073 K or lower, the intensity of the peaks at 284.1, 286.1, and 288.7 eV, originating from C–H, C–O/C=O, and COO, respectively, increased as the percentage of hydrogen and oxygen increased in Table  1 . The presence of lactone was also observed in IR spectra of CF 773 K and pitch after infusibilization (Fig.  12 a). FWHMs of each peak were set to be larger as the temperature decreased because the presence of a variety of the interactions with the different strengths as well as low conductivity causes a broadening of spectra. Sp 3 C–H is present in the samples prepared at 773 K or lower as exhibited in IR spectra (Fig.  12 b). However, the percentage of sp 3 C–H should be negligibly small at 1473 K or higher as shown in Fig.  12 b because of the thermal instability of sp 3 C–H [ 123 ,  124 ].

Figure  S20  shows C KLL  Auger spectra of samples and the D parameters obtained from the spectra are summarized in Table  S3 . In general, D parameters have been utilized to estimate the percentage of sp 3 C and sp 2 C [ 49 ,  155 ,  156 ] under the assumption that non-hexagonal rings and heteroatoms are either absent or irrelevant. Also, the usefulness of Auger spectra has been reported by our group using diamond embedded on HOPG [ 114 ]. In contrast, the ambiguity and the risks of this method to analyze the percentage of sp 3 C using the D parameter have been reported because the presence of various defects such as heteroatoms, crystallinity, and grain size in carbon materials [ 155 ], which relates to edges and non-hexagonal rings, and the synthesis conditions such as graphene on substrates [ 156 ], influences the D parameter other than sp 3 C. It is highly possible that the significant influence of non-hexagonal rings, heteroatoms, crystallinity, grain size, and synthesis conditions on the D parameters could cause an unreliable discussion of the percentage of sp 3 C. Moreover, since sp 3 C is unstable upon heat treatment in the absence of pressure [ 123 ,  124 ], the presence of sp 3 C should be negligible for carbon fiber heated at high temperatures under ambient pressure as shown in Fig.  12 b. From Table  S3 , the D parameter of CF 3173 K was not high (18 eV) in this work compared to that of HOPG (20.4 eV) in our previous work [ 114 ]. Assuming the reported relation between D parameter and the percentage can be applied to any carbon material, CF 3173 K should include full of sp 3 C, which would lead to misinterpretation. Since C KLL  Auger spectra cannot be calculated by our group, the details of the percentage of sp 3 C using C KLL  Auger spectra will not be discussed further.

The method conducted in this work is effective for roughly estimating the percentage of non-hexagonal rings in carbon materials prepared at high temperatures from the results of C1s XPS spectra. However, the accurate estimation of the peak position of C=C in hexagons is still challenging. Thus, combining XPS with combustion elemental analysis, Raman, and IR spectroscopy is essential to clarify the validity of the results of C1s XPS spectra. Also, it has to be kept in mind that some of the non-hexagonal rings cannot be differentiated from hexagonal rings since some of the peak positions of non-hexagonal rings are close to those of hexagonal rings.

sections.heading: XRD
paragraphs: Figures  16  and  S21  show the XRD patterns, lattice spacing ( d 002 ), and crystallite size ( L a) of pitch after infusibilization, CF prepared at 1073–3173 K, and flake graphite. These values are also summarized in Table  6 . The peaks at 2θ ≈ 25–26 and 28 degrees correspond to the (002) plane of graphite and the (110) plane of silicon used as a reference compound, respectively. As the heat treatment temperature increased from 1073 to 3173 K, the (002) peak position shifted to a higher angle and the FWHM decreased. This resulted in a larger crystallite size and smaller lattice spacing of the (002) plane. Although the lattice spacing of CF 3173 K was close to that of flake graphite, the crystallite size of CF 3173 K (4.16 nm) was much smaller than that of flake graphite (77.08 nm). In addition, the lattice spacing of CF 3173 K (0.3362 nm) is larger than that of flake graphite (0.3356 nm), which is close to that of the theoretical graphite structure (0.3354 nm), implying that the presence of non-hexagonal rings causes a non-planar structure [ 20 ]. Thus, it is clear that CF 3173 K contains more non-hexagonal rings, which generate non-planarity depending on the combination of hexagons and non-hexagons, than flake graphite, as indicated by the results of the Raman and C1s XPS spectra. The crystallite size remained small even after heat treatment at 3173 K (4.16 nm) compared with flake graphite (77.08 nm), suggesting that isotropic pitch, the carbon precursor of carbon fiber, has a structure in which various relatively small polycyclic aromatic molecules are randomly oriented. Consequently, it is difficult for crystallites to orient and grow even after heat treatment at high temperatures due to the formation of non-hexagonal rings. Thus, isotropic pitch is difficult to graphitize, similar to other non-graphitizing carbon materials [ 157 ]. sections.heading: Summary of structures
paragraphs: Figure  17  summarizes the estimated structures of isotropic pitch-based CF analyzed in this work, supported by previously reported results [ 31 ]. For comparison, the reported structures of PAN-based CF [ 20 ,  158 ] are also shown. Firstly, precursors were oxidized and further cross-linked with each other to maintain the fiber shape of CF even after carbonization/graphitization [ 31 ,  159 ]. Functional groups were mostly removed upon heat treatment, leaving a structure composed predominantly of carbon atoms. It is well known that the apparent density of PAN-based CF is 1.7–2.0 g cm −3  [ 160 ], whereas that of isotropic pitch-based CF is ca. 1.6 g cm −3 . Since the apparent densities of graphite (HOPG) and single-walled carbon nanotubes without opening their end caps have been reported to be 2.2 and 1.2 g cm −3 , respectively [ 161 ], both PAN-based and isotropic pitch-based CFs contain spaces. PAN-based CF prepared at 1873–2873 K contains non-hexagonal rings such as pentagons, heptagons, and octagons, along with a small amount of tertiary nitrogen in the basal plane (N/C: 0.001–0.004) [ 20 ]. In contrast, isotropic pitch-based CF prepared at 1873–2773 K in this work contains non-hexagonal rings such as pentagons, heptagons, and octagons in addition to cyclic ethers. Beyond the well-known structural differences, such as the connectivity and the aligned direction of crystallites along the fiber-axis direction, between PAN- and pitch-based CF, the difference in types of functional groups in the basal plane possibly contributes to the difference in mechanical strength. Tertiary nitrogen bonds with three carbon atoms, potentially enhancing mechanical strength, whereas cyclic ether bonds with two carbon atoms, potentially reducing it. However, this hypothesis requires future computational analysis for confirmation. Figure 17 Comparison of estimated structures between PAN-based CF [ 20 ,  158 ] and isotropic pitch-based CF in this work. Oxidized structures of PAN [ 91 ] and isotropic pitch [ 31 ] were obtained by referring from previous works.

Since the presence of non-hexagonal rings such as hexagon-heptagon rings [ 138 ] and functional groups [ 139 ] weakens the mechanical strength, researchers can optimize precursors and carbonization processes to selectively minimize these specific strength- or electrical conductivity-limiting defects by utilizing our clarified XPS and Raman/IR peak origins as quality-control metrics. Conversely, for energy storage applications or catalytic supports, specific topological defects such as pentagons and edge sites are highly desirable as active sites. Our findings allow researchers to use targeted spectroscopic peaks to intentionally maximize these specific active sites without degrading the highly conductive sp 2 C network. Thus, the investigation of defects by readily available spectroscopic analyses, such as Raman, IR, and XPS, will be further essential in the future.

sections.heading: Application of the results of this work to various carbon materials
paragraphs: The results obtained in this work provide basic guidelines for analyzing Raman and XPS spectra (Fig.  18 ) of various carbon materials with a small percentage of defects such as PAN-based CF, graphene, graphite, and other carbon materials prepared at high temperatures (1473 K or higher). For the other carbon materials with plenty of defects due to the low preparation temperatures, combination of Raman, IR, and XPS with NMR and molecular dynamics simulation with a reactive force field such as ReaxFF is essential because of the presence of various thermally unstable defects such as functional groups. For those materials, previously reported studies, such as infusibilized fiber precursor for pitch-based CF [ 31 ], graphene/graphite oxide [ 112 ], carbon materials with a high percentage of nitrogen [ 78 ,  92 ,  162 ]- or oxygen-containing functional groups [ 120 ,  141 ], carbon materials with edges [ 73 ], and carbon materials with high density pentagon or pentagon–heptagon [ 80 ,  81 ], are more suitable because those works studied specific structures with various defects that were not explained in this work. sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This work provides a foundation for the spectral analysis of isotropic pitch-based CF as an example of general carbon materials prepared at high temperatures, assisted by computational analyses. Throughout this study, the origin of the peak at ca. 285 eV for C1s XPS spectra, the trends of the peak shift in the C1s and N1s XPS spectra in the presence of non-hexagonal rings were revealed and the main origins of the D’ and G-band in Raman and the D’-like band in IR spectra were mainly clarified.

Regarding C1s XPS spectra, the origin of the peak at ca. 285 eV, which has been traditionally believed to be mainly originating from sp 3 C by many carbon material scientists, is revealed here to be a peak originating from the presence of non-hexagonal rings, if the peak does not originate from charged-up sp 3 C, C–N bonding, or adventitious carbon. It is because the peak of C1s XPS spectra of carbon materials with defects can reach 285.1 eV when the analyzed carbon atoms are surrounded by three rings, whose total summed number of surrounding three-membered rings is 20 ( e . g ., 6-6-8-membered rings). This result was obtained from the tendency for the peak position of C1s XPS spectra to shift higher as the total summed number increased. This work also reveals a clear trend that the peak position of N1s XPS spectra originating from tertiary nitrogen shifts to a higher binding energy as the total summed number of the surrounding three rings increases. These important results clarify the ambiguity of the assignment of XPS spectra of carbon materials such as isotropic pitch-based CF as shown in this work, leading to an estimation of the percentage of defects at 284.6 and 285.1 eV by C1s XPS spectra.

Moreover, the origin of the shifts in the Raman and IR spectra was clarified via theoretical calculations. For Raman and IR spectra, the peak shifts in the presence of various defects were explained by the bond length of C=C. The main origins of the D’ band of Raman spectra and the D’-like band of IR spectra for carbon materials were clarified as the presence of C=C at edges such as in DUO structures and that of a pentagon in the basal plane and on edges. The G -  band is influenced by non-hexagonal rings (such as eight-membered rings) and oxygen-containing functional groups. The intensity of A band is also influenced not only by non-hexagonal rings but also by oxygen-containing functional groups such as OH and cyclic ether groups. For IR spectra, the origin of the shift of SOLO in the presence of defects was explained by the change in the bond length of C=C bonded with sp 2 C–H. Through these analyses of Raman, IR, and XPS spectra, combined with combustion elemental analysis, it is clarified that CF heated at 1873–2773 K includes non-hexagonal rings such as pentagons, heptagons, and octagons in addition to a small percentage of edges and cyclic ether groups. For more precise analyses, combining these methods with other techniques, such as scanning tunneling microscopy, neutron scattering, and highly sensitive TPD, will be essential in the future since those techniques can confirm the presence of non-hexagonal rings and remaining edges.

It is expected that the approaches in this work supported by computational spectroscopic analyses will be applied for more precise spectral analysis of general carbon materials to improve their properties.
